quiz.q: CSF from a 22-year-old shows 240 WBC with 85% lymphocytes, glucose 62 mg/dL with a serum glucose of 98, and protein 58 mg/dL. Which diagnosis fits?
quiz.why: Lymphocytic pleocytosis with normal glucose is viral. Bacterial disease shows neutrophils with glucose under 40, and TB shows low glucose with very high protein.

quiz.q: Why is dexamethasone given with or before the first antibiotic dose in suspected pneumococcal meningitis?
choices: It improves antibiotic penetration across the blood-brain barrier
It blunts the inflammatory surge from bacterial cell wall fragments released during killing
It prevents the lumbar puncture headache
quiz.why: Antibiotic-induced lysis releases cell wall components that drive inflammation and hearing loss. Steroid given afterward misses that window and loses the benefit.

quiz.q: A 58-year-old has fever, confusion, aphasia, and a focal seizure. MRI shows temporal lobe changes. What should be started immediately?
quiz.why: Temporal lobe involvement with encephalopathy is HSV-1 encephalitis, and acyclovir must begin on suspicion because untreated mortality approaches 70 percent.

quiz.q: Which patient should have a CT scan before lumbar puncture?
choices: A 24-year-old with fever, headache and neck stiffness, alert and non-focal
A 30-year-old with a headache and a normal neurologic exam
A 19-year-old with photophobia and a normal fundoscopic exam
A 55-year-old with a new right-sided hemiparesis and papilledema
quiz.why: Focal deficits and papilledema raise the risk of herniation with a tap. The other three have no features suggesting a mass or elevated pressure.

quiz.q: A diabetic patient has a red, warm, tender lower leg with no fluctuance and no drainage. Temperature 37.8 C. Which is the best initial therapy?
quiz.why: Non-purulent cellulitis is predominantly streptococcal and treated with a first-generation cephalosporin. There is no collection to drain, no necrotizing red flags, and oral vancomycin is not absorbed systemically.

quiz.q: Which finding most strongly suggests necrotizing fasciitis rather than cellulitis?
choices: Warmth and erythema with poorly defined borders
Pain markedly out of proportion with crepitus and skin anesthesia
quiz.why: Disproportionate pain, gas in tissue and loss of sensation reflect fascial necrosis and nerve destruction. Warmth, mild fever and leukocytosis occur in ordinary cellulitis too.

quiz.q: A patient with sickle cell disease develops osteomyelitis. Which organism is characteristically added to the usual list?
quiz.why: Salmonella osteomyelitis is classically associated with sickle cell disease, though Staphylococcus aureus remains the overall most common cause. Pseudomonas is associated with puncture wounds through sneakers.

quiz.q: A 26-year-old has migratory joint pains, tenosynovitis of both wrists and scattered pustular skin lesions. Which diagnosis fits?
choices: Staphylococcal septic arthritis of the knee
quiz.why: The triad of migratory arthralgias, tenosynovitis and pustules is disseminated gonococcal infection. Staphylococcal disease is monoarticular, gout is podagra with crystals, and Lyme arthritis is a late monoarticular knee effusion.

quiz.q: A patient who injects drugs has fever, a new murmur, and septic pulmonary emboli on chest CT. Which valve and organism are most likely?
quiz.why: Right-sided tricuspid disease from Staphylococcus aureus sends emboli to the lungs rather than the brain or kidneys. Left-sided viridans disease follows dental procedures and embolizes systemically.

quiz.q: Four hours after a catered lunch, several guests develop sudden vomiting without fever. Which mechanism explains the timing?
choices: Invasion of the colonic mucosa by Shigella
A preformed enterotoxin already present in the food
Viral replication in enterocytes over 24 hours
Toxin production requiring 3 days of colonization
quiz.why: Onset within 1 to 6 hours is too fast for growth or invasion; the toxin was ingested ready-made, typically Staphylococcus aureus or Bacillus cereus.

quiz.q: A 6-year-old has bloody diarrhea after eating undercooked ground beef. Which management decision is correct?
choices: Give ciprofloxacin promptly to shorten illness
Give loperamide to reduce stool frequency
Withhold antibiotics and antimotility agents and monitor for hemolytic uremic syndrome
Give azithromycin and discharge without follow-up
quiz.why: Antibiotics and antimotility drugs in Shiga toxin-producing E. coli increase toxin exposure and hemolytic uremic syndrome risk. Supportive care with monitoring of hemoglobin, platelets and creatinine is correct.

quiz.q: Which hand hygiene method is required when caring for a patient with Clostridioides difficile?
choices: Alcohol rub followed by gloves only
No hand hygiene if gloves were worn
quiz.why: Alcohol does not kill C. difficile spores; mechanical removal with soap and water is required. Gloves are worn in addition, never instead.

quiz.q: Serology shows HBsAg positive, anti-HBc IgM positive, anti-HBs negative. Which interpretation is correct?
quiz.why: Surface antigen present with core IgM indicates recent, acute infection. Vaccination gives anti-HBs alone, and resolved infection gives anti-HBs with total anti-HBc.

quiz.q: Which hepatitis virus carries the highest risk of chronic infection after adult exposure?
quiz.why: Hepatitis C becomes chronic in roughly 75 to 85 percent of adults, versus about 5 percent for hepatitis B. Hepatitis A and E do not become chronic in immunocompetent hosts.

quiz.q: A homeless patient with HIV has a cough, night sweats and weight loss. A chest film shows a right apical cavity. What isolation is required at once?
choices: Airborne precautions with an N95 and negative-pressure room
quiz.why: Apical cavitation with this history is reactivation tuberculosis, and its droplet nuclei remain airborne for hours. A surgical mask and a standard room are insufficient.

quiz.q: Which antituberculous drug causes optic neuritis with loss of red-green discrimination?
quiz.why: Ethambutol is the eye drug. Isoniazid causes hepatitis and neuropathy, rifampin turns fluids orange and induces liver enzymes, pyrazinamide raises uric acid.

quiz.q: A patient with HIV and a CD4 count of 140 develops a dry cough and desaturates from 96% to 87% while walking. The chest film shows diffuse interstitial infiltrates. Most likely diagnosis?
quiz.why: Exertional desaturation with a diffuse interstitial pattern below CD4 200 is PCP. Toxoplasmosis is a brain disease below 100, and MAC is a disseminated febrile wasting illness below 50.

quiz.q: A nurse sustains a hollow-bore needlestick from a patient with untreated HIV. Which action is correct?
choices: Start three-drug post-exposure prophylaxis as soon as possible, within 72 hours
Wait for the nurse's baseline HIV test to return before starting anything
Give a single dose of antiretroviral therapy only
Start prophylaxis only if the source viral load exceeds 100,000
quiz.why: PEP is three drugs for 28 days and efficacy falls with every hour of delay. Baseline testing happens in parallel, and viral load thresholds do not gate the decision.

quiz.q: A 21-year-old has a purulent urethral discharge that began 4 days after a new partner. NAAT is pending. Which treatment is most appropriate now?
choices: Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM plus doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days
Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM
quiz.why: Purulent urethritis is gonococcal until proven otherwise, and chlamydial coinfection is common enough that both are covered. Penicillin treats syphilis and metronidazole treats trichomonas.

quiz.q: A patient develops fever, chills and myalgias several hours after benzathine penicillin for secondary syphilis. What is this?
choices: Treatment failure requiring a different antibiotic
quiz.why: The Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction is a self-limited inflammatory response to spirochete lysis, not an allergy. Anaphylaxis presents within minutes with airway and hemodynamic compromise.

quiz.q: A pregnant patient with penicillin allergy has primary syphilis. What is the correct management?
choices: Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 14 days
Penicillin desensitization followed by benzathine penicillin G
quiz.why: Only penicillin reliably treats fetal infection, so allergic pregnant patients are desensitized. Doxycycline is contraindicated in pregnancy and the alternatives have unacceptable failure rates.

quiz.q: A 33-year-old hiker in New Jersey has a 9 cm expanding red patch with central clearing and mild flu-like symptoms for 4 days. Lyme serology is negative. Best action?
choices: Treat with doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 10 to 14 days now
Repeat serology in 4 weeks before treating
quiz.why: Erythema migrans in an endemic area is a clinical diagnosis and early serology is frequently negative. IV ceftriaxone is reserved for carditis or neurologic disease.

quiz.q: A patient returns from West Africa with fevers for 3 days. There is no rash and no localizing findings. Which test is the priority?
choices: Thick and thin blood smears for malaria
quiz.why: Fever after travel to an endemic region is malaria until three negative smears 12 to 24 hours apart. Falciparum can kill within days, so it is ruled out first.

quiz.q: A patient wakes to find a bat in the bedroom. There is no visible bite. What is the correct management?
choices: Reassure; prophylaxis is needed only with a visible bite
Give rabies vaccine alone without immune globulin
Give rabies immune globulin 20 IU/kg plus vaccine on days 0, 3, 7 and 14
quiz.why: Bat exposures in a sleeping person count without a visible bite because bat bites can be imperceptible. The 10-day observation rule applies to dogs and cats, not wildlife.

quiz.q: A 26-year-old who is 24 weeks pregnant has no documented rubella immunity. What is the correct plan?
choices: Defer MMR until after delivery because it is a live vaccine
Give MMR only if she is exposed
quiz.why: Live attenuated vaccines are contraindicated in pregnancy, so MMR is given postpartum. Tdap and inactivated influenza vaccine, by contrast, are recommended during pregnancy.

quiz.q: Blood cultures in a stable, improving patient on meropenem grow Escherichia coli susceptible to ampicillin. What does stewardship require?
choices: Continue meropenem to complete the course
Narrow therapy to ampicillin or another narrow agent
quiz.why: De-escalation once susceptibilities return reduces resistance pressure, cost and adverse effects. Stopping early undertreats the bacteremia, and adding drugs is the opposite of stewardship.

scenarios.title: Triage: 71M, fever and confusion
scenarios.intro: A 71-year-old man is brought in by his daughter for two days of fever, shaking chills and worsening confusion. He had a urinary catheter placed last week after a prostate procedure. He takes lisinopril and metformin. He is warm, mottled at the knees, and answering only some questions.

steps.prompt: You are the first clinician at the bedside. The nurse has him on the monitor.

choices.text: Recognize sepsis: establish two large-bore IVs, draw blood cultures and a lactate, and start a 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus
choices.feedback: Correct. Altered mentation, RR 28 and SBP 86 make qSOFA 3 of 3. Access, cultures, lactate and fluid all start now.

choices.text: Give acetaminophen 650 mg and reassess the temperature in an hour
choices.feedback: Treating the number instead of the process. The fever is not what is going to kill him; the hypoperfusion is.

choices.text: Order a CT of the abdomen and pelvis first to find the source
choices.feedback: Imaging has a role, but a hypotensive septic patient does not leave the resuscitation bay before access, cultures and fluid.

choices.text: Obtain a urine culture only and wait for the result before doing anything else
choices.feedback: Harmful delay. Cultures are drawn alongside resuscitation, never instead of it.

steps.prompt: Two IVs are in. The lactate returns at `4.6 mmol/L`. Blood cultures from two sites are drawn. The catheter bag holds cloudy, foul urine.

choices.text: Give broad-spectrum antibiotics now, within the first hour, targeting a catheter-associated urinary source
choices.feedback: Right. Each hour of delay in septic shock measurably raises mortality. Cultures were already drawn, so nothing is lost.

choices.text: Hold antibiotics until the urine culture identifies the organism
choices.feedback: Cultures take a day or more. Empiric therapy starts now and is narrowed later.

choices.text: Give antibiotics but only after the full fluid bolus has finished infusing
choices.feedback: Fluids and antibiotics run in parallel, not in sequence. Sequencing them wastes the hour that matters.

steps.prompt: The `30 mL/kg` bolus is complete. He is more awake but still not at baseline. Repeat lactate is `3.8 mmol/L`.

choices.text: Start norepinephrine and titrate to a mean arterial pressure of 65 mmHg
choices.feedback: Correct. Hypotension persisting after adequate fluid defines septic shock and calls for a vasopressor. Norepinephrine is first line.

choices.text: Give another 3 liters of crystalloid rapidly and reassess in an hour
choices.feedback: Additional fluid may be reasonable in small aliquots, but unlimited crystalloid causes pulmonary edema. After the initial bolus fails, pressors are the answer.

choices.text: Start dopamine for its renal protective effect
choices.feedback: Renal-dose dopamine is a discredited idea and dopamine causes more arrhythmias than norepinephrine.

choices.text: Accept the pressure as his baseline and move him to the hallway
choices.feedback: A MAP in the 50s with a lactate of 3.8 is ongoing tissue hypoperfusion, not a baseline.

steps.prompt: He is on norepinephrine with a MAP of `68 mmHg` and is admitted to the intensive care unit. The team asks about the catheter that was placed last week.

choices.text: Remove or replace the catheter as part of source control
choices.feedback: Correct. Antibiotics cannot sterilize a colonized device. Source control is as important as the drug.

choices.text: Leave the catheter in place; antibiotics will clear it
choices.feedback: Biofilm on the catheter shelters organisms from antibiotics and reseeds the bladder.

choices.text: Leave the catheter and add a second antipseudomonal agent instead
choices.feedback: Adding drugs in place of source control broadens resistance without solving the problem.

scenarios.debrief: The pattern: fever plus altered mentation plus hypotension in a patient with an indwelling device is sepsis from a catheter-associated urinary source until proven otherwise. The sequence never changes. Lactate and cultures, antibiotics inside one hour, `30 mL/kg` crystalloid, then norepinephrine to a MAP of `65 mmHg` if the pressure stays down. Source control closes the loop: remove the infected hardware, because no antibiotic penetrates a biofilm reliably. Imaging and definitive diagnosis happen alongside resuscitation, never before it.

scenarios.title: Reasoning through a febrile returning traveler
scenarios.intro: A 29-year-old returns from three weeks in rural Ghana visiting family. Eight days after arriving home she has fevers to `39.4 C`, headache, and body aches. No rash, no cough, no diarrhea. She took a malaria prophylaxis prescription but admits she stopped it after the first week. Work through the reasoning one decision at a time.

steps.prompt: First framing question: what is the single diagnosis you must exclude before anything else?

choices.text: Malaria, because falciparum can kill within days and this is an endemic-area exposure
choices.feedback: Correct. Fever plus travel to an endemic area means malaria first. Stopping prophylaxis early removes the main protection she had.

choices.text: Influenza, since fever and body aches are classic
choices.feedback: The symptoms do overlap, but influenza does not kill this patient in 48 hours and malaria might. Rank by lethality, not by frequency alone.

choices.text: Lyme disease, given the headache and myalgias
choices.feedback: Lyme is a North American tick exposure with a rash stage. It does not explain a Ghana travel history.

choices.text: Viral upper respiratory infection; reassure and discharge
choices.feedback: Discharging an undifferentiated post-travel fever without a malaria smear is how falciparum deaths happen.

steps.prompt: You order the right test. The first set of thick and thin blood smears is reported as negative. She still has a temperature of `39.1 C`.

choices.text: Repeat smears at 12 to 24 hour intervals, up to three sets, before calling malaria excluded
choices.feedback: Correct. Parasitemia is cyclic and a single negative smear does not rule out malaria. Three negatives over 48 hours are required.

choices.text: Declare malaria excluded and move on to other causes
choices.feedback: One negative smear is not exclusion. This is the most common error in this presentation.

choices.text: Start empiric antimalarial therapy without further testing
choices.feedback: Understandable in a critically ill patient, but this patient is stable and the species and parasite density change the drug choice.

steps.prompt: While the second smear is pending, you build a parallel differential for post-travel fever. Which additional feature would most change your thinking toward dengue?

choices.text: Retro-orbital headache, severe bone pain, a falling platelet count and a rash
choices.feedback: Correct. Dengue incubates 4 to 7 days and gives retro-orbital pain, breakbone myalgias, thrombocytopenia and hemoconcentration.

choices.text: Upper lobe cavitation on chest film
choices.feedback: That points at tuberculosis, which is a slower, weeks-long illness with weight loss and night sweats.

choices.text: A migrating red patch with central clearing on the thigh
choices.feedback: That is erythema migrans, which belongs to Lyme disease, not a tropical febrile illness.

choices.text: Painless genital ulcer
choices.feedback: That is primary syphilis and does not explain daily high fevers after travel.

steps.prompt: The second smear shows ring forms with a parasitemia of `2%`, consistent with *Plasmodium falciparum*. She is alert, tolerating oral intake, with normal renal function and no acidosis.

choices.text: Admit, treat as falciparum malaria with a species-appropriate regimen, and monitor for cerebral malaria, hypoglycemia and rising parasitemia
choices.feedback: Correct. Falciparum is treated and watched closely because deterioration can be rapid even when the initial presentation looks stable.

choices.text: Discharge on oral therapy with follow-up in one week
choices.feedback: Falciparum with 2 percent parasitemia can worsen quickly. Follow-up in a week is too late to catch it.

choices.text: Treat with doxycycline alone and reassess in 48 hours
choices.feedback: Doxycycline is a partner drug and a prophylactic agent, not adequate monotherapy for acute falciparum infection.

scenarios.debrief: The pattern to keep: fever plus travel equals malaria until three thick and thin smears say otherwise, and one negative smear excludes nothing because parasitemia is cyclic. Rank the differential by what kills fastest, not by what is most common. Dengue is the parallel consideration, distinguished by retro-orbital pain, breakbone myalgias and falling platelets, and it is the one where aspirin and NSAIDs are avoided. Falciparum earns admission even when the patient looks well, because cerebral malaria, hypoglycemia and rising parasitemia appear faster than a follow-up appointment.
